transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-06-02 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~58 minutes
Attendees: Sofia Martinez (Redwood AE), Ethan Li (Redwood SE), Priya Ramanathan (Head of ML, Nimble), Marcus Lee (CTO, Nimble), Dana Ortiz (Platform Lead, Nimble)

[00:00] Sofia (Redwood AE): hey everyone thanks for joining, um we'll keep this pretty focused on reliability and incident tolerance for your LLM inference needs. quick intro — im sofia, i'm the AE on the account, and with me is ethan our solutions engineer.
[00:12] Priya (Nimble): thanks sofia, yep i'm priya, we run the ml stack here, marcus and dana are with me. gotta say we've been looking at hosted vs dedicated vs an on prem/private deployment for some of our customer facing chat and personalization flows.
[00:25] Marcus (Nimble CTO): happy to be here, short timeline — we want a PoC by june end and hopefully roll out in q3 if perf looks good. main thing is reliability and how you handle incidents.
[00:37] Ethan (Redwood SE): awesome. can you share current traffic and SLOs? even ballpark QPS, p95 latency targets, and what failures you worry most about?
[00:45] Dana (Platform): so day to day we're seeing 1.2k requests/min peak on promo days, average 300/min. target p95 < 400ms for simple text gen endpoints; for chat flow p95 < 800ms. we also need 99.95% availability for customer-facing endpoints — that's our internal SLO.
[01:05] Priya: also multi-region — we have NA + EU customers and a few APAC pilot markets. data residency is a concern for EU payments flows.
[01:12] Sofia: got it. two parts to the reliability conversation: 1) what happens during an incident (fallbacks, graceful degradation, routing), and 2) operational guarantees and SLAs (uptime, support, runbooks).
[01:25] Ethan: quick note on terminology — when i say fallback i mean automated alternatives: model variant fallback (smaller or quantized model), regional fallback, and cached response fallback (prefix/kv cache).
[01:35] Marcus: spelled that out helps. our main worry is a region-wide outage or sudden throughput spike. we need decisions on cross-region failover, and whether requests can failover within 100-200ms without toot much cost.
[01:48] Sofia: right. for Hosted we do smart routing by default: requests route to nearest region, with policy rules you can set for latency vs cost. if a region is unhealthy we reroute to another region and can optionally fallback to a cheaper model variant. there is a small added latency for inter-region failover — typically additional network hop plus cold-start of new instance if not warm.
[02:10] Priya: how do you warm things? does dedicated keep pools hot?
[02:14] Ethan: Dedicated pools are reserved GPU pools with configurable autoscaling and warm instances; you can set policy for warm standbys per region. Hosted has warm workers too but they are multi-tenant so warm-up may be slightly slower when scaling from zero for large spikes.
[02:30] Dana: what about KV cache behavior across regions? we want cached responses to persist and be available even after a region fails.
[02:36] Ethan: currently cache is per-region by default to keep consistency and low latency; cross-region cache replication is available as an opt-in config for Dedicated/Private deployments but with tradeoffs (eventual consistency, higher egress). we sometimes see transcriptions list it as K V cash in notes — ha.
[02:55] Marcus: ha. ok. that replication is interesting. can you make it synchronous?
[02:59] Ethan: synchronous RPC across regions increases latency significantly; we recommend async replication plus a policy for fallback to model variant or cached stubs. many customers set a short TTL plus replication behind a best-effort sync for warmups.
[03:15] Priya: on the SLA side — do you offer SLA tiers on Hosted? Dedicated?
[03:19] Sofia: Hosted comes with a baseline SLA for availability (we quoted 99.9% for our platform plan historically), but for enterprise customers we offer Dedicated with higher SLA options and contractual uptime targets (99.95% or 99.99%) as part of reserved capacity agreements. Private deployments — those are self-hosted control plane, so SLA is more about support and response SLAs from Redwood rather than an availability SLA for the compute you manage.
[03:43] Marcus: what's the latency SLA look like? we typically don't get latency SLAs from vendors but we need internal SLO alignment.
[03:50] Sofia: we publish performance profiles per model/region and can create a contract addendum for latency SLOs tied to Dedicated capacity and warm-standby policies.
[03:59] Dana: ok. say a region goes down — what's the typical RTO and RPO for your fallbacks?
[04:05] Ethan: RTO depends on policy: for automated regional failover to a warm pool in another region it's typically seconds to tens of seconds — if a warm standby exists. If we need to spin up capacity in a different region cold, that can be a few minutes. RPO for data/cache depends on replication settings; default per-region cache means RPO is region-limited, but with replication you'll get near-zero RPO for critical keys (again eventual consistency caveat).
[04:30] Priya: sounds reasonable. any automated traffic shaping during incidents? like degrade complexity or cutoff tokens?
[04:36] Ethan: yes — Redwood can apply graceful degradation policies: reduce max tokens, use smaller model variant, enable prefix cache-only responses for known prompts, and circuit-breaker style queuing with priority lanes for important traffic. Those are configurable per-route.
[04:53] Marcus: can we run a policy that allows checkout flows to be high priority while personalization is best-effort?
[04:58] Sofia: absolutely — routing and priority lanes are per-API-key or per-route. you can set fallthrough routes, and if a primary region is degraded, checkout requests can failover to Dedicated cold or even to a small but highly-available family of models with a slightly different prompt.
[05:15] Dana: who manages the failover rules during an incident? ops or does Redwood auto decide?
[05:20] Ethan: we provide both: automatic health-driven routing with policy defaults, and an ops console where your Platform team can override. For Dedicated/Private, you can choose fully managed automatic failovers or a semi-auto mode requiring approval.
[05:33] Priya: security and compliance — we need SOC2 type2, KMS integration, SSO/SAML, audit trails. is that available across modes?
[05:43] Sofia: yes. Hosted supports SOC2 and KMS integrations for customer-managed keys (depending on plan), SSO/SAML and RBAC for the console. Dedicated includes additional audit log retention and can be deployed with VPC peering. Private gives you full network control and on-prem options and lets you plug into HSMs. We'll share the security pack.
[06:02] Marcus: perfect. how about data residency for EU payments flows? we need EU-only processing and logs kept in EU.
[06:09] Ethan: we'd recommend Dedicated with per-region isolation or Private. For Hosted we have region pinning, but logs sometimes flow to control plane in another region for analytics. For strict residency you should choose Dedicated or Private and we can provide region-isolated logging and KMS in the target region.
[06:28] Priya: curious about cost tradeoffs. if we keep warm standbys in two regions for failover, that's double capacity cost, right?
[06:34] Sofia: yes that's the tradeoff — higher cost for lower RTO. You can minimize cost by keeping small warm pools and relying on quantized smaller variants as intermediate fallbacks. Redwood Optimize tooling can help recommend a good balance given your workload.
[06:49] Marcus: what about multi-region active-active vs active-passive? we prefer active-active for latencies but concerned about state and cache coherence.
[06:58] Ethan: active-active is supported but requires careful cache/shard strategy. For session state we recommend sticky routing with region affinity for most users, and cross-region session replication for critical flows. Active-passive simplifies cache coherence and reduces cross-region egress. We'll share architecture patterns we've implemented (we'll send a doc).
[07:18] Dana: any real customer examples of multi-region failover?
[07:21] Ethan: yes — one retailer we work with had region failover tested during a maintenance window; they used Dedicated with warm standbys and saw sub-100ms impact for most endpoints. we can anonymize and share that runbook.
[07:33] Priya: ok let's talk specifics we need in the PoC: 1) benchmark with our dataset and UI flows 2) simulate NA region outage and measure failover time and latency 3) test global cache replication behavior and consistency 4) evaluate cost delta for warm-standby scenario.
[07:51] Sofia: good checklist. ethan will own the benchmarking and we'll need your team to provide sample traffic and a few representative prompts.
[07:58] Ethan: yes, please send a sanitized dataset and traffic trace. we'll run with a 5k QPS simulation and share p50/p95/p99 and failover timelines.
[08:08] Marcus: timeline — can you get results back in ~1 week?
[08:11] Ethan: initial synthetic runs in 3 business days; full run with failover simulation and cost analysis in 7-10 days.
[08:19] Priya: good. one more question — how do you handle telemetry and tracing during incidents? we need request-level tracing and token-level cost breakdown.
[08:27] Sofia: Redwood Console includes request tracing, per-token cost breakdown, and per-route dashboards. we can forward traces to your datadog or new relic. audit logs and request bodies are optional to retain for compliance.
[08:40] Dana: retention — can we set log retention longer for billing/audit?
[08:44] Sofia: yes, Dedicated and Private have extended retention options as an add-on. Hosted has tiered retention.
[08:51] Marcus: how are fallbacks surfaced to the app? is there an explicit flag that a response is degraded? we need to show users when answers are from a cached stub or reduced model.
[08:59] Ethan: yes — response metadata includes model_version, fallback_reason (if any), and a confidence tag. you can use that to annotate UI. sometimes transcription will show this as "fallback: cache" or similar.
[09:12] Priya: would be helpful to have a canary or dark launch behavior for fallbacks so we can test without affecting production.
[09:18] Sofia: we support canary routes and A/B rollouts — canary traffic, percentage-based rollouts, and automatic rollback if quality/regression checks fail.
[09:28] Marcus: last operational question: who leads an incident? is there a joint runbook?
[09:33] Ethan: for Redwood-managed Dedicated we have an incident response playbook and an on-call engineer. you'll get a single point of contact during the PoC and a joint postmortem process. for Private it's collaborative — we provide runbooks and support tiers.
[09:48] Priya: ok sounds like you cover the bases. any limitations or gotchas we should be aware of?
[09:53] Ethan: a few: cross-region cache sync is eventual not strongly consistent; cold-starts can be a few minutes without warm-standbys; cost for multi-region warm capacity can be high; and some model variants have different perf profiles so fallback can change output quality — which you'll want to monitor with evals.
[10:13] Sofia: to recap the ask: Nimble wants a PoC to validate failover behaviour, SLO alignment, and cost delta between single-region with large capacity vs multi-region with warm standby. next steps: 1) Sofia sends pricing + security pack 2) Ethan sets up benchmark harness + schedule 3) Priya shares sanitized data and SLOs 4) set PoC kickoff for week of 2027-06-14.
[10:37] Marcus: that's perfect. also please include a short note on regional data residency and audit log retention options in your security pack.
[10:44] Sofia: will do. any other questions?
[10:47] Dana: none from me. thanks.
[10:49] Priya: thanks, appreciate it.
[10:52] Sofia: thanks all, we'll follow up via email and put the PoC doc and runbook in the thread.
[10:57] (call ends)
